notes.front: In a built-in continuous-flow system, what sets the final flow rate at each user station, and why do crew masks differ?
notes.back: A calibrated orifice in each mask; crew masks usually have larger orifices for greater flow.
notes.explanation: Special masks with even larger orifices serve passengers with medical conditions needing full blood saturation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Continuous-Flow Systems”, p. 16-8
notes.evidence: Built-in continuous-flow gaseous oxygen systems accomplish a final flow rate to individual user stations through the use of a calibrated orifice in each mask. Larger diameter orifices are usually used in crew masks to provide greater flow than that for passengers.

notes.front: How does a rebreather bag or cannula reduce waste in a continuous-flow system?
notes.back: It captures exhaled oxygen so it can be inhaled with the next breath.
notes.explanation: Exhaled air still contains usable oxygen, so lower flow rates are enough.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Continuous-Flow Systems”, p. 16-8
notes.evidence: Oxygen and air that is exhaled still contains usable oxygen. By capturing this oxygen in a bag, or in a cannula with oxygen absorbing reservoirs, it can be inhaled with the next breath, reducing waste.

notes.front: In an emergency continuous-flow passenger system, what turns on the oxygen to an individual deployed mask?
notes.back: Pulling the mask toward the passenger, which pulls a lanyard attached to it.
notes.explanation: Depressurisation deploys the masks automatically from the overhead passenger service unit; the crew can also deploy them.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Continuous-Flow Systems”, p. 16-8
notes.evidence: When used as an emergency system in pressurized aircraft, depressurization automatically triggers the deployment of oxygen ready continuous-flow masks at each passenger station. A lanyard attached to the mask turns on the flow to each mask when it is pulled toward the passenger for use.

notes.front: How do continuous-flow oxygen masks fit, and what do their vent holes do?
notes.back: They fit snugly but are not airtight; vent holes mix cabin air with the oxygen and let exhaled air escape.
notes.explanation: They are simple devices that just direct the flow to the nose and mouth.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Continuous-Flow Systems”, p. 16-9
notes.evidence: Continuous-flow oxygen masks are simple devices made to direct flow to the nose and mouth of the wearer. They fit snugly but are not air tight. Vent holes allow cabin air to mix with the oxygen and provide escape for exhalation.

notes.front: Why does a demand-flow oxygen supply last longer than a continuous-flow supply?
notes.back: Oxygen flows only as the user inhales and stops during the hold and exhalation periods.
notes.explanation: None of the oxygen is wasted while the user is not drawing a breath.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-9
notes.evidence: When oxygen is delivered only as the user inhales, or on demand, it is known as a demand-flow system or a pressure-demand system. During the hold and exhalation periods of breathing, the oxygen supply is stopped. Thus, the duration of the oxygen supply is prolonged as none is wasted.

notes.front: In a demand-flow system, the pressure-reducing valve lowers cylinder pressure to roughly {{c1::60–85 psi}} before the individual regulators.
notes.explanation: A further reduction happens at each regulator’s small inlet orifice.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: This device lowers the oxygen pressure from the storage cylinder(s) to roughly 60–85 psi and delivers it to individual regulators dedicated for each user. A pressure reduction also occurs at the inlet of the individual regulator by limiting the size of the inlet orifice.

notes.front: At approximately what altitude does a diluter-demand regulator meter 100 percent oxygen?
notes.back: About 34,000 feet.
notes.explanation: As altitude rises, an aneroid lets more oxygen and less cabin air through; full oxygen should not be needed unless pressurisation fails.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: As altitude increases, an aneroid allows more oxygen and less cabin air to be delivered to the user by adjusting flows through a metering valve. At approximately 34,000 feet, the diluter-demand regulator meters 100 percent oxygen. This should not be needed unless cabin pressurization fails.

notes.front: What does the built-in emergency switch on a diluter-demand regulator deliver?
notes.back: 100 percent oxygen in a continuous flow, bypassing the demand function.
notes.explanation: The user can also select 100 percent oxygen at any time with the oxygen selection lever, which keeps the demand function.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: Additionally, the user may select 100 percent oxygen delivery at any time by positioning the oxygen selection lever on the regulator. A built-in emergency switch also delivers 100 percent oxygen, but in a continuous flow as the demand function is bypassed.

notes.front: On what aircraft are pressure-demand regulators used, and why?
notes.back: Aircraft that regularly fly at 40,000 feet and above; forcing oxygen in under pressure ensures blood saturation at any altitude.
notes.explanation: They also appear on many airliners and high-performance aircraft that may not usually fly that high.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: Pressure-demand regulators are used on aircraft that regularly fly at 40,000 feet and above. They are also found on many airliners and high-performance aircraft that may not typically fly that high. Forcing oxygen into the lungs under pressure ensures saturation of the blood, regardless of altitude or cabin altitude.

notes.front: Why must demand-flow oxygen masks be close fitting?
notes.back: So that inhaling creates low pressure in the regulator, which lets oxygen flow.
notes.explanation: Exhaled air leaves through ports in the mask, and the regulator stops the flow until the next breath.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Figure 16-19”, p. 16-11
notes.evidence: Demand-flow masks are close fitting so that when the user inhales, low pressure is created in the regulator, which allows oxygen to flow. Exhaled air escapes through ports in the mask, and the regulator ceases the flow of oxygen until the next inhalation.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, up to what altitude do continuous-flow oxygen systems protect passengers?
notes.back: Up to 25,000 feet above mean sea level.
notes.explanation: The AC notes they give a continuous flow of 100 percent oxygen and may be automatic or manual.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4.6.1, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: Continuous-flow oxygen systems provide protection for passengers up to 25,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) and a continuous flow of 100 percent oxygen to the user. They may be automatic or manual in their operation.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, what oxygen system must aircraft certified to operate above 25,000 feet have for required crewmembers?
notes.back: A demand system.
notes.explanation: The AC cites part 23 (§ 23.1441) as the source of this requirement.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4.6.3, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: Title 14 CFR § 23.1441 requires aircraft that are certified to operate above 25,000 feet to be equipped with a demand system to supply required crewmembers.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, which aircraft must have a pressure-demand oxygen system?
notes.back: Aircraft certified to exceed 40,000 feet.
notes.explanation: The AC says the type is not likely on small general aviation models.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4.6.4, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: This type is not likely to be included on small general-aviation models. Aircraft certified to exceed 40,000 feet must have a pressure-demand system,

notes.front: A crew mask regulator gives nothing until the wearer inhales, then mixes cabin air with oxygen, adding more oxygen as the cabin altitude climbs. Which type is it?
notes.back: B) Diluter-demand
notes.choices:
A) Continuous-flow
B) Diluter-demand
C) Pressure-demand
D) Chemical generator
notes.choicesExplained: A flows all the time, even during exhalation. C pushes oxygen in under pressure rather than only diluting it. D gives a fixed continuous flow once lit.
notes.explanation: Holding back flow until inhalation and diluting with cabin air according to cabin altitude is what defines the diluter-demand regulator.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: The diluter-demand type regulator holds back the flow of oxygen until the user inhales with a demand-type oxygen mask. The regulator dilutes the pure oxygen supply with cabin air each time a breath is drawn.

notes.front: A business jet routinely cruises at 45,000 feet. Which crew oxygen regulator type suits it?
notes.back: A) Pressure-demand
notes.choices:
A) Pressure-demand
B) Manual continuous-flow
C) Diluter-demand only
D) A portable rebreather cannula
notes.choicesExplained: B is a light-aircraft arrangement that wastes oxygen and does not force it into the lungs. C only dilutes and depends on the wearer drawing oxygen in. D is a low-altitude continuous-flow device.
notes.explanation: Pressure-demand regulators are used on aircraft that regularly fly at 40,000 feet and above, because forcing oxygen in ensures saturation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Demand-Flow or Pressure-Demand Systems”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: Pressure-demand regulators are used on aircraft that regularly fly at 40,000 feet and above.

notes.front: A light aircraft carries a portable cylinder with a regulator on the bottle, a hose and a cannula. With the valve open, oxygen flows even while the pilot breathes out. Which system type is this?
notes.back: C) Continuous-flow
notes.choices:
A) Diluter-demand
B) Pressure-demand
C) Continuous-flow
D) Onboard oxygen generating system
notes.choicesExplained: A and B both stop the flow during exhalation. D separates oxygen from engine bleed air on military aircraft.
notes.explanation: Flow that continues while the user exhales is the mark of a continuous-flow system; the handbook uses a light aircraft portable set as its example of the type.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Continuous-Flow Systems”, p. 16-7
notes.evidence: Once the valve is opened, the flow of oxygen is continuous. Even when the user is exhaling, or when the mask is not in use, a preset flow of oxygen continues until the tank valve is closed.

notes.front: In continuous-flow systems, what second job do many flow meters do?
notes.back: They double as flow rate adjusters.
notes.explanation: Needle valves fitted in the indicator housing give fine adjustment of the delivery rate.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Flow Indicators”, p. 16-10
notes.evidence: When flow exists, this movement signals the user in some way. [Figure 16-23] Many flow meters in continuous-flow oxygen systems also double as flow rate adjusters. Needle valves

notes.front: Where are flow indicators usually found in demand-flow systems, and what are two ways they show flow?
notes.back: Built into each user’s regulator; some blink when oxygen is delivered, others move a coloured pith object into a window.
notes.explanation: Whatever the design, they give a quick check that the system is working.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Flow Indicators”, p. 16-12
notes.evidence: Demand-flow oxygen systems usually have flow indicators built into the individual regulators at each user station. Some contain a blinking device that activates when the user inhales and oxygen is delivered. Others move a colored pith object into a window. Regardless, flow indicators provide a quick verification that an oxygen system is functioning.

notes.front: What are the three acceptable means AC 43.13-2C gives for indicating oxygen flow to each user?
notes.back: Listening for audible flow; watching a rebreather or reservoir bag inflate; installing a flow indicator.
notes.explanation: The AC also accepts an equivalent means.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.8.7, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: 1. Listening for audible indication of oxygen flow. 2. Watching for inflation of the rebreather or reservoir bag. 3. Installing a flow indicator.

notes.front: What does an electronic pulse-demand unit fitted to a continuous-flow system do?
notes.back: It delivers timed pulses of oxygen only when an inhalation starts.
notes.explanation: This saves the oxygen that would otherwise be lost during the hold and exhale parts of each breath.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Flow Indicators”, p. 16-12
notes.evidence: It delivers timed pulses of oxygen to the wearer on demand, saving oxygen normally lost during the hold and exhale segments of the breathing cycle. Advanced pressure sensing and processing allows the unit to deliver oxygen only when an inhalation starts.

notes.front: What material are high-pressure oxygen lines usually made of, and what is typical for low-pressure tubing?
notes.back: High-pressure lines are usually stainless steel; low-pressure tubing is typically aluminium.
notes.explanation: Most lines in permanent installations are metal; flexible plastic hose is used to carry oxygen to the masks.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-14
notes.evidence: Most lines are metal in permanent installations. High-pressure lines are usually stainless steel. Tubing in the low-pressure parts of the oxygen system is typically aluminum.

notes.front: How is installed oxygen tubing usually identified?
notes.back: Tape at each end and along its length: a green band printed with the words breathing oxygen, and a black rectangle on a white border strip.
notes.explanation: The colour-coded tape goes on each end of the tubing and at specified intervals along it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-14
notes.evidence: Installed oxygen tubing is usually identified with colorcoded tape applied to each end of the tubing, and at specified intervals along its length. The tape coding consists of a green band overprinted with the words “BREATHING OXYGEN” and a black rectangular symbol overprinted on a white background border strip.

notes.front: The five valve types common in high-pressure gaseous oxygen systems are filler, check, {{c1::shutoff}}, pressure reducer and pressure relief.
notes.explanation: They work as in any other system, except that oxygen shutoff valves are designed to open slowly.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-14
notes.evidence: Five types of valves are commonly found in high-pressure gaseous oxygen systems: filler, check, shutoff, pressure reducer, and pressure relief. They function as they would in any other system with one exception: oxygen system shutoff valves are specifically designed to open slowly.

notes.front: What happens when high-pressure oxygen rushes into a low-pressure area and meets an obstruction such as a valve seat?
notes.back: It compresses (adiabatic compression) and gets hot enough to exceed the ignition point of materials.
notes.explanation: The rushing oxygen can reach the speed of sound, and the ignition point of any substance is lower in pure oxygen than in air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-14
notes.evidence: The ignition point for any substances is lower in pure oxygen than it is in air. When high-pressure oxygen is allowed to rush into a low-pressure area, its velocity could reach the speed of sound. If it encounters an obstruction (a valve seat, an elbow, a piece of contaminant, etc.), the oxygen compresses.

notes.front: Can a stainless-steel line ignite in an oxygen system?
notes.back: Yes: under high pressure and temperature in 100 percent oxygen, even stainless steel can ignite.
notes.explanation: The same line would not normally burn when carrying other fluids at high pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: A stainless-steel line, for example, would not normally burn and is used for carrying numerous fluids under high pressure. But under high pressure and temperature in the presence of 100 percent oxygen, even stainless steel can ignite.

notes.front: Why are oxygen shutoff valves slow-opening, and how should technicians open every oxygen valve?
notes.back: To decrease the oxygen’s velocity; technicians should always open all oxygen valves slowly.
notes.explanation: Slowing the flow prevents the rapid compression heating that can start a fire or explosion.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: To combat this issue, all oxygen shutoff valves are slow, opening valves designed to decrease velocity. [Figure 16-27] Additionally, technicians should always open all oxygen valves slowly.

notes.front: What features slow the flow and ensure full closure in a typical high-pressure oxygen shutoff valve?
notes.back: Fine-pitch threads and a regulating stem to slow the flow, and a soft seat so it closes completely.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s example valve is built to open gradually rather than snap open.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Figure 16-27”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: This high-pressure oxygen system shutoff valve has fine-pitch threads and a regulating stem to slow the flow of oxygen through the valve. A soft valve seat is also included to assure the valve closes completely.

notes.front: After replacing a regulator, a technician is about to open the cylinder valve into the empty lines of a high-pressure oxygen system. How should it be opened?
notes.back: B) Slowly, to keep the oxygen’s velocity down
notes.choices:
A) Quickly, so the lines fill before any moisture enters
B) Slowly, to keep the oxygen’s velocity down
C) Quickly, then back it off a quarter turn
D) Slowly only if the lines are aluminium
notes.choicesExplained: A and C both let oxygen rush into the low-pressure lines, the condition that causes compression heating. D is wrong because the rule applies to all oxygen valves, and even stainless steel can ignite.
notes.explanation: Oxygen rushing into a low-pressure area can compress at an obstruction and heat past the ignition point of materials.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: Additionally, technicians should always open all oxygen valves slowly. Keeping oxygen from rushing into a lowpressure area should be a major concern when working with high-pressure gaseous oxygen systems.

notes.front: What does a missing green blowout disc on the fuselage skin near an oxygen installation mean?
notes.back: The oxygen system’s relief valve has opened; the cause should be investigated before flight.
notes.explanation: The relief valve is ported to the disc, which sits where a walk-around inspection will see it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: Often, the valve is ported to an indicating or blowout disc. This is located in a conspicuous place, such as the fuselage skin, where it can be seen during walk-around inspection. Most blowout discs are green. The absence of the green disc indicates the relief valve has opened, and the cause should be investigated before flight.

notes.front: On a walk-around, a mechanic sees that the green disc beside the crew oxygen servicing panel on the fuselage is missing. What does this show?
notes.back: D) The oxygen system’s pressure relief has discharged overboard; investigate before flight
notes.choices:
A) The engine fire extinguisher bottle has discharged
B) The cabin pressurisation safety valve has opened
C) The oxygen cylinder is below 50 psi
D) The oxygen system’s pressure relief has discharged overboard; investigate before flight
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses the oxygen disc with fire bottle indicators; this one is ported from the oxygen relief valve. B vents cabin air through its own valve, not this disc. C would show on the pressure gauge, not by a blown disc.
notes.explanation: The oxygen relief valve is ported to the green disc, so its absence means the relief valve opened.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen Plumbing & Valves”, p. 16-15
notes.evidence: Oxygen cylinder valves and high-pressure systems are often provided with a relief valve should the desired pressure be exceeded. Often, the valve is ported to an indicating or blowout disc.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, what typical cause of excess pressure does the relief valve guard against in a low-pressure oxygen system, and in a high-pressure one?
notes.back: Low-pressure: overcharging. High-pressure: heating.
notes.explanation: Both systems carry a relief valve; the AC names a different typical cause for each.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4.8, p. 7-4
notes.evidence: 7.4.8.1 A relief valve is installed in low-pressure oxygen systems to safely relieve excessive pressure, such as that caused by overcharging. 7.4.8.2 A relief valve is installed in high-pressure oxygen systems to safely relieve excessive pressure, such as that caused by heating.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, at what pressures is oxygen stored in high-pressure and low-pressure gaseous systems?
notes.back: High-pressure: 1,850 psi. Low-pressure: 425 psi.
notes.explanation: The AC says every oxygen system has a storage tank, a regulation system and a distribution system.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Gaseous oxygen systems may be a higher-pressure system with oxygen stored at 1,850 pounds per square inch (psi) or a low-pressure system with the oxygen stored at 425 psi. All oxygen systems contain a storage tank, a regulation system, and a distribution system.

notes.front: Why does AC 43.13-2C say titanium fittings should never be used in high-pressure oxygen systems?
notes.back: Because of a possible chemical reaction and resulting fire.
notes.explanation: The AC also discourages mild steel or aluminium alloy fittings with stainless steel lines.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.4.3.1, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Mild steel or aluminum alloy fittings with stainless steel lines are discouraged. Titanium fittings should never be used because of a possible chemical reaction and resulting fire.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, how should oxygen lines, fittings and equipment be placed relative to fuel, oil and hydraulic systems?
notes.back: Above them and at least 6 inches away.
notes.explanation: Deflector plates are used where needed to keep hydraulic fluid off oxygen parts.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.5.5, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: Install lines, fittings, and equipment above and at least 6 inches away from fuel, oil, and hydraulic systems. Use deflector plates where necessary to keep hydraulic fluids away from the lines, fittings, and equipment.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, what clearance should oxygen plumbing have from flexible control cables, and from rigid control tubes?
notes.back: At least 2 inches from flexible cables and moving parts; at least 1/2 inch from rigid control tubes and moving parts.
notes.explanation: Flexible parts move about more, so they get the larger gap.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.5.6, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: Allow at least a 2-inch clearance between the plumbing and any flexible control cable or other flexible moving parts of the aircraft. Provide at least a 1/2-inch clearance between the plumbing and any rigid control tubes or other rigid moving parts of the aircraft.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, how much clear airspace should there be between an oxygen cylinder and a firewall or shroud isolating a fire zone?
notes.back: At least 1/2 inch.
notes.explanation: The AC also wants the cylinder shutoff valve reachable from inside the cabin in flight.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.6.4, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: Provide at least 1/2-inch of clear airspace between any cylinder and a firewall or shroud isolating a designated fire zone.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, where is oxygen thread compound applied on a tapered pipe fitting?
notes.back: Sparingly, only to the male threads, coating the first three threads from the end of the fitting.
notes.explanation: Compound is kept off coupling sleeves and the outside of tube flares.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.7.3, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: Make sure that the compounds are carefully and sparingly applied only to male threads, coating the first three threads from the end of the fitting. Do not use compound on the coupling sleeves or on the outside of the tube flares.

notes.front: Should thread compound be used on aluminium alloy flared tube fittings with straight threads in an oxygen system?
notes.back: No; proper flaring and tightening should make the joint leakproof.
notes.explanation: Compound is meant for tapered pipe threads, not straight-thread flared joints.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.7.1, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: Do not use compound on aluminum alloy flared tube fittings having straight threads. Proper flaring and tightening should be sufficient to make a flared tube connection leakproof.

notes.front: Why must typical thread sealers not be used on oxygen pipe fittings?
notes.back: They are petroleum based; only oxygen-compatible lubricants or sealers may be used.
notes.explanation: Pure oxygen combines violently with petroleum products.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Replacing Tubing, Valves, & Fittings”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: This type of connection is usually sealed with the application of thread lubricant/sealant. Typical thread sealers are petroleum based and should not be used; only oxygen compatible thread lubricant/sealers should be used.

notes.front: When Teflon tape is used on an oxygen pipe fitting, where should the wrapping begin, and why?
notes.back: At least two threads from the end of the fitting, so no tape can come loose and enter the system.
notes.explanation: Loose tape inside an oxygen system is a contaminant.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Replacing Tubing, Valves, & Fittings”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Be sure to begin wrapping the Teflon® tape at least two threads from the end of the fitting. This prevents any tape from coming loose and entering the oxygen system.

notes.front: How should new oxygen tubing be cleaned before installation?
notes.back: Flushed with nonpetroleum cleaners such as trichlorethylene or acetone, then blown or baked dry.
notes.explanation: New tubing often carries residue from bending or flaring.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Replacing Tubing, Valves, & Fittings”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Often tubing comes with leftover residue from the bending or flaring processes. Cleaning should be accomplished with nonpetroleum-based cleansers. Trichlorethylene, acetone, and similar cleaners can be used to flush new tubing. Tubing should be blown or baked dry before installation.

notes.front: A mechanic is fitting a tapered pipe-thread elbow into an oxygen regulator. Which sealing method is correct?
notes.back: B) Oxygen-compatible compound, sparingly, on the first three male threads only
notes.choices:
A) Petroleum-based pipe dope on all threads
B) Oxygen-compatible compound, sparingly, on the first three male threads only
C) Teflon tape wrapped from the very first thread
D) Compound on the female threads inside the regulator
notes.choicesExplained: A uses a petroleum-based sealer, which must not be used. C lets tape come loose into the system; wrapping starts at least two threads back. D puts compound where it should not go; it belongs only on male threads.
notes.explanation: The AC limits compound to male threads, coated sparingly on the first three threads from the end.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.7.3, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: Make sure that the compounds are carefully and sparingly applied only to male threads, coating the first three threads from the end of the fitting.

notes.front: What should be used to find leaks in a gaseous oxygen system?
notes.back: Oxygen-safe leak check fluid: a soapy liquid free of anything that might react with pure oxygen; bubbles show a leak.
notes.explanation: It is applied to the outside of fittings and mating surfaces, as with a tyre.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Testing Gaseous Oxygen Systems”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: Detection of leaks should be performed with oxygen-safe leak check fluid. This is a soapy liquid free from elements that might react with pure oxygen or contaminate the system. As with leak detection on an inflated tire or tube assembly, the oxygen leak detection solution is applied to the outside of fittings and mating surfaces. The formation of bubbles indicates a leak.

notes.front: Why can leaks in a continuous-flow oxygen system be hard to find, and what helps?
notes.back: The system is open at the user end; blocking the flow lets pressure build for a leak check.
notes.explanation: With pressure held, the checks used on the high-pressure sections can then be followed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Testing Gaseous Oxygen Systems”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: Leaks in a continuous-flow oxygen system may be difficult to detect because the system is open at the user end. Blocking the flow of oxygen allows pressure to build and leak check procedures can be followed that are similar to those used in the high-pressure sections of the systems.

notes.front: An oxygen fitting still leaks although it is torqued correctly. What must be done?
notes.back: Release system pressure, examine the fitting for flaws or contamination, and replace it if necessary.
notes.explanation: Tightening may not always stop a leak, so more torque is not the answer.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Testing Gaseous Oxygen Systems”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: torqued properly and a leak still exists, pressure must be released from the system and the fitting must be examined for flaws or contamination. If necessary, the fitting must be replaced.

notes.front: Should a leaking oxygen fitting be tightened while the system is pressurised or charging?
notes.back: No; isolate the oxygen in the cylinder and depressurise the system first.
notes.explanation: Depressurising reduces the consequences of a spark and limits injury if the fitting fails completely.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Testing Gaseous Oxygen Systems”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: No attempt should be made to tighten a leaky oxygen fitting while the system is charging. The oxygen supply should be isolated in the cylinder and the system depressurized to reduce the consequences of a spark or to minimize spillage and injury should a complete fitting failure occur.

notes.front: How can a technician identify the high-pressure section of a gaseous oxygen system?
notes.back: It is the part upstream of the reducer or regulator, with stainless steel tubing.
notes.explanation: With the tank valve open, this section can hold up to 1,850 psi.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Testing Gaseous Oxygen Systems”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: An open tank valve pressurizes the lines and components with up to 1,850 pounds per square inch (psi) of oxygen. Identify the high-pressure section of the system as that portion upstream of the reducer or regulator that has stainless steel tubing.

notes.front: What is the basic procedure for draining an oxygen system?
notes.back: Establish a continuous flow in a safe area, preferably outside, until the system is empty.
notes.explanation: The main concern is releasing the oxygen without causing a fire, explosion or other hazard.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Draining an Oxygen System”, p. 16-16
notes.evidence: The biggest factor in draining an oxygen system is safety. The oxygen must be released into the atmosphere without causing a fire, explosion, or hazard. Draining outside is highly recommended. The exact method of draining can vary. The basic procedure involves establishing a continuous flow in a safe area until the system is empty.

notes.front: When filling an aircraft oxygen system, why should valves be opened slowly and filling proceed slowly?
notes.back: To avoid overheating.
notes.explanation: The fill hose is also purged of air before use, and pressures are checked often during refilling.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-17
notes.evidence: Oxygen valves should be opened slowly, and filling should proceed slowly to avoid overheating. The hose from the refill source to the oxygen fill valve on the aircraft should be purged of air before it is used to transfer oxygen into the system. Pressures should also be checked frequently while refilling.

notes.front: Before using an oxygen filler cart, what three things should be checked about its cylinders?
notes.back: They hold aviator's breathing oxygen, each holds at least 50 psi, and each is within its hydrostatic test date.
notes.explanation: Recording each cylinder’s remaining pressure after use lets the next technician see its status at a glance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-17
notes.evidence: Be sure all cylinders on the cart are aviator’s breathing oxygen and that all cylinders contain at least 50 psi of oxygen pressure. Each cylinder should also be within its hydrostatic test date interval.

notes.front: How does oxygen move from a filler cart into the aircraft cylinder without a pump?
notes.back: By pressure difference: cart cylinders of increasingly higher pressure are opened one at a time.
notes.explanation: Gas flows from high to low pressure, so opening them in rising order gives a slow, managed increase in flow.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-17
notes.evidence: No pump or mechanical device is used to transfer oxygen from the fill cart manifold to the aircraft system. Objects under pressure flow from high pressure to low pressure. Thus, by connecting the cart to the aircraft and systematically opening oxygen cylinders with increasingly higher pressure, a slow increase in oxygen flow to the aircraft can be managed.

notes.front: In the handbook’s oxygen refill procedure, what is done to the filler cart just before its hose is connected to the aircraft?
notes.back: It is grounded to the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The hose is then purged of air with oxygen before the aircraft refill valve is opened.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-17
notes.evidence: 4. Ground the refill cart to the aircraft. 5. Connect the cart hose from the cart manifold to the aircraft fill port. Purge the air from the refill hose with oxygen before opening the refill valve on the aircraft.

notes.front: An aircraft oxygen cylinder reads 600 psi. The filler cart has cylinders at 400, 900, 1,500 and 2,000 psi. Which cart cylinder should be opened first?
notes.back: B) 900 psi
notes.choices:
A) 400 psi
B) 900 psi
C) 1,500 psi
D) 2,000 psi
notes.choicesExplained: A is below the aircraft cylinder, so oxygen would not flow into the aircraft. C and D exceed it by more than necessary, giving a faster, hotter fill than the step-by-step method intends.
notes.explanation: The procedure opens the cart cylinder with the closest pressure that exceeds the aircraft cylinder, then the next highest.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-17
notes.evidence: Observe the pressure on the aircraft bottle to be filled. Open it. On the refill cart, open the cylinder with the closest pressure to the aircraft cylinder that exceeds it.

notes.front: On a hot day, why may oxygen cylinders be filled above their standard 1,800 or 1,850 psi rating?
notes.back: Because at altitude the oxygen’s temperature and pressure can fall significantly.
notes.explanation: Filling to the temperature-compensated value ensures a full supply is available when needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: When it is hot, oxygen cylinders are filled to a higher pressure than 1,800 psi or 1,850 psi, the standard maximum pressure ratings of most high-pressure aircraft oxygen cylinders. This is allowable because at altitude the temperature and pressure of the oxygen can decrease significantly.

notes.front: On a cold day, how full should oxygen cylinders be filled, and why?
notes.back: To less than their maximum rated capacity, allowing for pressure increases as the temperature rises.
notes.explanation: Strict adherence to the temperature and pressure chart is mandatory for safe storage.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: When filling cylinders on a cold day, compensation for temperature and pressure changes dictates that cylinders be filled to less than the maximum rated capacity to allow for pressure increases as temperature rises.

notes.front: Using the refill chart shown, a technician fills a cylinder whose line is labelled “1,800 at 70 °F” on a day of about 104 °F (40 °C). What should the gauge pressure be?
notes.back: C) More than 1,800 psi
notes.choices:
A) Less than 1,800 psi
B) Exactly 1,800 psi
C) More than 1,800 psi
D) Nothing: filling above 86 °F is not allowed
notes.choicesExplained: A is the cold-day case, to the left of the 70 °F line. B applies only at 70 °F. D is not in the chart, which runs to 140 °F.
notes.explanation: Each line rises to the right: hotter days call for higher fill pressures, as the handbook allows.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: Technicians should consult the chart and fill cylinders to the maximum pressure listed for the prevailing ambient temperature. [Figure 16-32] When it is hot, oxygen cylinders are filled to a higher pressure than 1,800 psi or 1,850 psi,

image.alt: A chart of gauge pressure in hundreds of psi, 7 to 20, against temperature from –40 to 140 °F (–40 to 60 °C). Ten parallel lines slope upward to the right, labelled 900 at 70 °F up to 1,800 at 70 °F. A red vertical line marks 70 °F. On the 1,800 line, pressure is below 1,800 psi to the left of 70 °F and above it to the right.
image.credit: FAA, FAA-H-8083-31B Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe, Figure 16-32

notes.front: How does a refill valve with built-in temperature compensation work?
notes.back: The ambient temperature is set on the valve dial, and the valve closes when the correct pressure is reached in the cylinder.
notes.explanation: A chart can still be used to confirm proper servicing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Filling an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: Some aircraft have temperature compensation features built into the refill valve. After setting the ambient temperature on the valve dial, the valve closes when the correct amount of oxygen pressure has been established in the aircraft cylinder.

notes.front: An oxygen system needs to be purged if it has been opened or depleted for more than {{c1::2 hours}}, or if contamination is suspected.
notes.explanation: Purging removes contaminants and restores oxygen saturation inside the system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: An oxygen system needs to be purged if it has been opened or depleted for more than 2 hours, or if it is suspected that the system has been contaminated.

notes.front: What is the main cause of contamination in an oxygen system?
notes.back: Moisture.
notes.explanation: It can come from condensation in very cold weather, from air entering an opened system, or from damp charging equipment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: The main cause of contamination in an oxygen system is moisture. In very cold weather, the small amount of moisture contained in the breathing oxygen can condense.

notes.front: How long is oxygen generally run through a system to purge it?
notes.back: As little as 10 minutes at normal delivery pressure; some systems need up to 30 minutes at elevated pressure.
notes.explanation: The procedure varies by aircraft model, so the maintenance manual governs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging an Oxygen System”, p. 16-18
notes.evidence: Generally speaking, oxygen is run through a sound oxygen system for a number of minutes at a given pressure to perform the purging. This can be as little as 10 minutes at normal delivery pressure. Other systems may require up to 30 minutes of flow at an elevated pressure.

notes.front: Nitrogen or dry air may be blown through oxygen lines during maintenance. What is required before the system is serviceable?
notes.back: A final purge with pure oxygen.
notes.explanation: Cylinders used up in purging must be refilled, and all safety caps fitted, before return to service.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging an Oxygen System”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: and components when performing maintenance. However, a final purging with pure oxygen is required before the system is serviceable for use.

notes.front: A crew oxygen system was left open for 3 hours during a regulator change, and the lines were blown through with dry nitrogen. What must happen before return to service?
notes.back: B) Purge with pure oxygen, refill the cylinder, then leak check
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more, as dry nitrogen has already cleaned the lines
B) Purge with pure oxygen, refill the cylinder, then leak check
C) Purge with dry air for 30 minutes
D) Fill to pressure; the oxygen itself will displace the nitrogen in use
notes.choicesExplained: A skips the required final oxygen purge. C uses dry air, which is acceptable only for blowing through during maintenance, not for the final purge. D skips purging for a system open more than 2 hours.
notes.explanation: A system open over 2 hours must be purged, the final purge must be pure oxygen, and a leak check follows any opening of the system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging an Oxygen System”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: However, a final purging with pure oxygen is required before the system is serviceable for use. It is important to ensure storage cylinders are refilled if they are used during the purging process.

notes.front: When inspecting oxygen masks and hoses, which defects are unacceptable and how are they usually remedied?
notes.back: Leaks, holes and tears; usually by replacing the damaged unit.
notes.explanation: Mask and hose integrity ensures oxygen actually reaches the user, sometimes in an emergency.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: Mask and hose integrity ensure effective delivery of oxygen to the user when it is needed. Sometimes this is in an emergency situation. Leaks, holes, and tears are not acceptable. Most discrepancies of this type are remedied by replacement of the damaged unit.

notes.front: What may be used to clean reusable oxygen masks?
notes.back: Mild cleaners and antiseptics that are free of petroleum products.
notes.explanation: Clean masks reduce the danger of infection and last longer; some continuous-flow masks are disposable instead.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: Masks designed to be reused should be clean, as well as functional. This reduces the danger of infection and prolongs the life of the mask. Various mild cleaners and antiseptics that are free of petroleum products can be used.

notes.front: Some continuous-flow masks are disposable. What must the technician make sure of?
notes.back: That there is a mask for each potential user on board.
notes.explanation: A mask thrown away after use must be replaced before the next flight needs it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: Some continuous-flow masks are designed for disposal after use. Be sure there is a mask for each potential user on board the aircraft.

notes.front: How do continuous-flow mask hoses differ from demand-flow mask hoses, and why?
notes.back: They are much smaller in diameter, because the hose’s inside diameter helps control the flow rate.
notes.explanation: Masks for each kind of system are made to connect only to the proper hose.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: The diameter of mask hoses in a continuous-flow system is quite a bit smaller than those used in a demand-flow system. This is because the inside diameter of the hose aids in controlling flow rate. Masks for each kind of system are made to only connect to the proper hose.

notes.front: On which aircraft are smoke masks required, and what do they cover?
notes.back: Transport aircraft; they cover the eyes as well as the nose and mouth.
notes.explanation: Their hoses plug into the same demand regulator port as regular demand masks.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: Smoke masks are required on transport aircraft and are used on some other aircraft as well. These cover the eyes, as well as the user’s nose and mouth.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, how is oxygen availability checked at each diluter-demand regulator?
notes.back: Turn the lever to “100 percent oxygen” and inhale through the mask to see that the regulator valve and flow indicator work.
notes.explanation: Measuring each outlet’s flow is unnecessary because the regulator maker supplies the flow characteristics.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.8.6.4, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: However, in such systems, the availability of oxygen to each regulator should be checked by turning the lever of the diluter-demand regulator to the “100 percent oxygen” position and inhaling through the tube via the mask to determine whether the regulator valve and the flow indicator are operating.

notes.front: During an inspection, a mechanic finds a small tear in the hose of a crew quick-donning oxygen mask. The mask still delivers oxygen. What is the usual remedy?
notes.back: D) Replace the damaged unit
notes.choices:
A) Patch the tear with adhesive tape
B) Seal it with petroleum-based sealant
C) Leave it until the next inspection
D) Replace the damaged unit
notes.choicesExplained: A is out because adhesive tape is not to be used on oxygen equipment. B brings petroleum into contact with oxygen. C accepts a tear, which is not acceptable.
notes.explanation: Leaks, holes and tears are unacceptable, and most are remedied by replacing the damaged unit.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Inspection of Masks & Hoses”, p. 16-19
notes.evidence: Leaks, holes, and tears are not acceptable. Most discrepancies of this type are remedied by replacement of the damaged unit.

notes.front: Before any work on an oxygen system, what should be on hand and how should the area be prepared?
notes.back: An adequate fire extinguisher on hand; the area cordoned off with no-smoking placards posted.
notes.explanation: Tools and equipment should be clean, and power-on checks and use of the aircraft electrical system avoided.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Prevention of Oxygen Fires or Explosions”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Before any work is attempted, an adequate fire extinguisher should be on hand. Cordon off the area and post “NO SMOKING” placards. Ensure that all tools and servicing equipment are clean and avoid power on checks and use of the aircraft electrical system.

notes.front: There should be absolutely no smoking or open flames within a minimum of {{c1::50}} feet of oxygen system work.
notes.explanation: Clean, grease-free hands, clothes and tools are also essential, ideally with tools kept only for oxygen work.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Clean, grease-free hands, clothes, and tools are essential. A good practice is to use only tools dedicated for work on oxygen systems. There should be absolutely no smoking or open flames within a minimum of 50 feet of the work area.

notes.front: What should be used to close off open oxygen cylinders, components and plumbing, and what must not be used?
notes.back: Protective caps and plugs; no adhesive tape of any kind.
notes.explanation: AC 43.13-2C likewise says not to use tape, rags or paper on open tubing ends.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Always use protective caps and plugs when working with oxygen cylinders, system components, or plumbing. Do not use any kind of adhesive tape.

notes.front: Where should oxygen cylinders be stored in the hangar?
notes.back: In a designated, cool, ventilated area away from petroleum products and heat sources.
notes.explanation: Heat raises cylinder pressure, and petroleum reacts violently with oxygen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Oxygen cylinders should be stored in a designated, cool, ventilated area in the hangar away from petroleum products or heat sources.

notes.front: Before oxygen system maintenance begins, what must be done, and how should fittings be undone?
notes.back: Close the supply cylinder valve and release system pressure; unscrew fittings slowly.
notes.explanation: Undoing fittings slowly lets any residual pressure dissipate.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: Oxygen system maintenance should not be accomplished until the valve on the oxygen supply cylinder is closed and pressure is released from the system. Fittings should be unscrewed slowly to allow any residual pressure to dissipate.

notes.front: How much clearance should oxygen lines have from moving parts, electrical wiring and fluid lines?
notes.back: At least 2 inches.
notes.explanation: Clearance is also needed from hot ducts and anything else that might heat the oxygen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-21
notes.evidence: 2 inches of clearance from moving parts, electrical wiring, and all fluid lines. Adequate clearance must also be provided from hot ducts and other sources that might heat the oxygen.

notes.front: When must a pressure and leak check be done on an oxygen system?
notes.back: Each time the system is opened for maintenance.
notes.explanation: Lubricants, sealers and cleaners are used only if specifically approved for oxygen systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-21
notes.evidence: A pressure and leak check must be performed each time the system is opened for maintenance. Do not use any lubricants, sealers, cleaners, etc., unless specifically approved for oxygen system use.

notes.front: A mechanic plans to replace an oxygen line in the hangar. A colleague is welding about 30 feet away, and the mechanic wants aircraft power on to test the regulator heater during the job. What should change?
notes.back: B) Stop the welding within 50 feet and avoid power-on checks while the system is open
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if a fire extinguisher is nearby
B) Stop the welding within 50 feet and avoid power-on checks while the system is open
C) Move the welding to 20 feet away behind a screen
D) Carry on, but use adhesive tape to seal the open line ends
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the open flame inside 50 feet and the power-on check. C brings the flame even closer. D adds a second error: adhesive tape must not be used.
notes.explanation: The handbook requires no open flames within at least 50 feet and says to avoid power-on checks and use of the aircraft electrical system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Oxygen System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 16-20
notes.evidence: There should be absolutely no smoking or open flames within a minimum of 50 feet of the work area.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-2C, what hazard do pressurised oxygen cylinder failures present, especially with aluminium-lined composite cylinders?
notes.back: They can produce violent explosions.
notes.explanation: The AC lists this among the hazards to consider when installing an oxygen system.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.2.4, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Pressurized oxygen cylinder failures, particularly aluminum-lined composite cylinders, have the potential of producing violent explosions.

notes.front: An oxygen duration placard, based on a fully charged 48 cubic-foot cylinder, shows 5.07 hours for a pilot and one passenger at 8,000 feet. The aircraft actually has a full 63 cubic-foot cylinder. About how long will the oxygen last?
notes.back: C) About 6.6 hours
notes.choices:
A) About 3.9 hours
B) About 5.1 hours
C) About 6.6 hours
D) About 10.1 hours
notes.choicesExplained: A divides by 1.3 instead of multiplying. B ignores the larger cylinder. D doubles the figure, which the AC does not say to do.
notes.explanation: The AC’s table note says to multiply any duration by 1.3 for a 63 cubic-foot cylinder; 5.07 × 1.3 ≈ 6.6.
notes.source: AC 43.13-2C, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Alterations (29 July 2026), Chapter 7, Oxygen System Installations in Nonpressurized Aircraft, 7.9, Table 7-1, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: NOTE: The above duration time is based on a fully charged 48 cubic-foot cylinder. For duration using a 63 cubic-foot cylinder, multiply any duration by 1.3.

notes.front: Why is atmospheric pressure at sea level said to be 14.7 psi?
notes.back: A one-square-inch column of air from sea level into space weighs 14.7 pounds.
notes.explanation: The gases of the atmosphere are invisible but have weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressure of the Atmosphere”, p. 16-21
notes.evidence: The gases of the atmosphere (air), although invisible, have weight. A one square inch column of air stretching from sea level into space weighs 14.7 pounds. Therefore, it can be stated that the pressure of the atmosphere, or atmospheric pressure, at sea level is 14.7 psi.

notes.front: In hectopascals, the unit now nearly universal in meteorology, 14.7 psi is equal to {{c1::1,013.2}} hPa.
notes.explanation: A hectopascal is a metric unit of force in newtons per square metre.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressure of the Atmosphere”, p. 16-21
notes.evidence: However, the unit of force nearly universally used today to represent atmospheric pressure in meteorology is the hectopascal (hPa). A hectopascal is a metric (SI) unit that expresses force in newtons per square meter. 1,013.2 hPa is equal to 14.7 psi.

notes.front: What is atmospheric pressure at 40,000 feet, compared with 14.7 psi at sea level?
notes.back: About 2.72 psi.
notes.explanation: Pressure falls rapidly with height; by 50,000 feet it is almost one-tenth of the sea level value.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Figure 16-37”, p. 16-21
notes.evidence: Figure 16-37. Atmospheric pressure decreasing with altitude. At sea level the pressure is 14.7 psi, while at 40,000 feet, as the dotted lines show, the pressure is only 2.72 psi.

notes.front: In the troposphere, at about what rate does temperature fall with height, and what is the temperature at the tropopause?
notes.back: About –2 °C (–3.5 °F) per 1,000 feet; about –57 °C (–69 °F) at the tropopause.
notes.explanation: Most civil flying takes place in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Temperature & Altitude”, p. 16-22
notes.evidence: The rate of change is somewhat constant at about –2 °C or –3.5 °F for every 1,000 feet of increase in altitude. The upper boundary of the troposphere is the tropopause. It is characterized as a zone of relatively constant temperature of –57 °C or –69 °F.

notes.front: A cabin altitude of 8,000 feet corresponds to a cabin pressure of {{c1::10.92}} psi.
notes.explanation: The handbook uses this value when describing how a crew selects a cabin altitude in isobaric mode.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Modes”, p. 16-27
notes.evidence: For example, the flight crew may select to maintain a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet (10.92 psi).

notes.front: According to the handbook, what cabin pressure altitude must a pressurisation system be able to maintain, and why?
notes.back: About 8,000 feet or lower at any cruising altitude, so occupants get enough oxygen at enough pressure for full blood saturation.
notes.explanation: It must also prevent rapid cabin pressure changes and circulate air to remove odours and stale air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Issues”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: It must be capable of maintaining a cabin pressure altitude of approximately 8,000 feet or lower regardless of the cruising altitude of the aircraft. This is to ensure that passengers and crew have enough oxygen present at sufficient pressure to facilitate full blood saturation.

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(a), pressurised cabins must provide a cabin pressure altitude of not more than {{c1::8,000 feet}} under normal operating conditions.
notes.explanation: This applies to pressurised cabins and compartments to be occupied on transport category aeroplanes.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(a), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: (a) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, pressurized cabins and compartments to be occupied must be equipped to provide a cabin pressure altitude of not more than 8,000 feet under normal operating conditions.

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(a)(1), if certification above 25,000 feet is requested, what cabin pressure altitude must occupants not exceed after any probable pressurisation failure?
notes.explanation: This is a failure limit, separate from the 8,000-foot normal-operations limit.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(a)(1), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: (1) If certification for operation above 25,000 feet is requested, the airplane must be designed so that occupants will not be exposed to cabin pressure altitudes in excess of 15,000 feet after any probable failure condition in the pressurization system

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(a)(2), after decompression from a failure not shown to be extremely improbable, what cabin pressure altitudes must occupants not be exposed to?
notes.back: Above 25,000 feet for more than 2 minutes, or above 40,000 feet for any time.
notes.explanation: Fuselage structure, engine and system failures are all considered in judging the decompression.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(a)(2), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: (2) The airplane must be designed so that occupants will not be exposed to a cabin pressure altitude that exceeds the following after decompression from any failure condition not shown to be extremely improbable: (i) Twenty-five thousand (25,000) feet for more than 2 minutes; or (ii) Forty thousand (40,000) feet for any duration.

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(b)(1), how many pressure relief valves must a pressurised cabin have to limit positive differential, and how big must they be together?
notes.back: Two, with enough combined capacity that failure of any one causes no appreciable rise in differential.
notes.explanation: The differential is positive when the internal pressure is greater than the external.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(b)(1), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: (1) Two pressure relief valves to automatically limit the positive pressure differential to a predetermined value at the maximum rate of flow delivered by the pressure source. The combined capacity of the relief valves must be large enough so that the failure of any one valve would not cause an appreciable rise in the pressure differential.

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(b)(2), what must automatically prevent a damaging negative pressure differential?
notes.back: Two reverse pressure differential relief valves or equivalents; one is enough if its design reasonably precludes malfunction.
notes.explanation: The structure is designed for cabin pressure to exceed outside pressure, not the reverse.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(b)(2), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: (2) Two reverse pressure differential relief valves (or their equivalents) to automatically prevent a negative pressure differential that would damage the structure. One valve is enough, however, if it is of a design that reasonably precludes its malfunctioning.

notes.front: Under 14 CFR 25.841(b)(6), above what cabin pressure altitude must an alert warn the flight crew?
notes.explanation: Warning markings on the differential pressure indicator can meet the warning requirement for differential limits.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(b)(6), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: An alert meets the warning requirement for cabin pressure altitude limits if it warns the flightcrew when the cabin pressure altitude exceeds 10,000 feet,

notes.front: A proposed transport category design holds a 9,000-foot cabin altitude at its normal cruise. Does it meet 14 CFR 25.841(a)?
notes.back: B) No, because under normal conditions the cabin must be at not more than 8,000 feet
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the limit is 10,000 feet
B) No, because under normal conditions the cabin must be at not more than 8,000 feet
C) Yes, if it stays below 15,000 feet after a failure
D) Yes, because only the rate of change is regulated
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses the 10,000-foot crew alert with the normal limit. C quotes the probable-failure limit, which is a separate requirement. D is wrong because the rule sets a cabin altitude limit.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (a) caps cabin pressure altitude at 8,000 feet under normal operating conditions.
notes.source: 14 CFR 25.841(a), Pressurized cabins (govinfo, 1 January 2025 edition)
notes.evidence: pressurized cabins and compartments to be occupied must be equipped to provide a cabin pressure altitude of not more than 8,000 feet under normal operating conditions.

notes.front: What is cabin rate of climb, and in what units is it expressed?
notes.back: The rate of change of air pressure inside the cabin, in feet per minute of cabin altitude change.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the handbook’s key pressurisation terms, alongside cabin altitude and differential pressure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Terms”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: Cabin rate of climb—the rate of change of air pressure inside the cabin, expressed in feet per minute (fpm) of cabin altitude change.

notes.front: Typical rates of change for cabin pressure are {{c1::300 to 500}} feet per minute.
notes.explanation: The rate can be controlled automatically or manually by the flight crew.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Modes”, p. 16-28
notes.evidence: This can be done automatically or manually by the flight crew. Typical rates of change for cabin pressure are 300 to 500 fpm.

notes.front: An aircraft cruises at 30,000 feet, where ambient pressure is 4.37 psi, with a cabin altitude of 6,000 feet (11.77 psi). What is the cabin differential pressure?
notes.back: B) 7.40 psid
notes.choices:
A) 4.37 psid
B) 7.40 psid
C) 11.77 psid
D) 16.14 psid
notes.choicesExplained: A is just the ambient pressure. C is just the cabin pressure. D adds the two instead of subtracting.
notes.explanation: Differential is cabin pressure minus ambient pressure: 11.77 − 4.37 = 7.40 psid.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Terms”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: Cabin pressure (psi) – ambient pressure (psi) = cabin differential pressure (psid or Δ psi).

notes.front: Over what range does cabin differential pressure run, from light to high-performance aircraft?
notes.back: From about 3.5 psi on a single-engine piston aircraft to about 9 psi on high-performance jets.
notes.explanation: The fuselage must withstand this pressure difference, which makes weight the design challenge.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Issues”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: A key factor in pressurization is the ability of the fuselage to withstand the forces associated with the increase in pressure inside the structure versus the ambient pressure outside. This differential pressure can range from 3.5 psi for a singleengine reciprocating aircraft, to approximately 9 psi on high performance jet aircraft.

notes.front: What parts of an aircraft does the sealed pressure vessel usually include?
notes.back: The cabin, the flight compartment and the baggage compartments.
notes.explanation: Door seals, grommets and sealants together make these areas airtight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Issues”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: Compressible seals around doors combine with various other seals, grommets, and sealants to essentially establish an air tight pressure vessel. This usually includes the cabin, flight compartment, and the baggage compartments.

notes.front: Air is pumped into the pressure vessel at a constant rate. How then is cabin pressure controlled?
notes.back: By adjusting the rate at which air is allowed to flow out of the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The inflow is set slightly above what is needed, so the outflow does the controlling.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Issues”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: Air is then pumped into this area at a constant rate sufficient to raise the pressure slightly above that which is needed. Control is maintained by adjusting the rate at which the air is allowed to flow out of the aircraft.

notes.front: What effect do repeated pressurisation and depressurisation cycles have on the airframe, and what FAA response does the handbook mention?
notes.back: Metal fatigue that weakens the airframe; the FAA’s aging aircraft program increased inspection of older airframes.
notes.explanation: Some early pressurised aircraft failed from this fatigue, with fatal results.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Pressurization Issues”, p. 16-23
notes.evidence: metal fatigue from repeated pressurization and depressurization weakens the airframe. Some early pressurized aircraft structures failed due to this and resulted in fatal accidents. The FAA’s aging aircraft program was instituted to increase inspection scrutiny of older airframes that may show signs of fatigue due to the pressurization cycle.

notes.front: What are the three typical sources of air used to pressurise reciprocating-engine aircraft?
notes.back: Supercharger, turbocharger and engine-driven compressor.
notes.explanation: Superchargers and turbochargers boost induction air, and some of that air can be routed to the cabin.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Aircraft”, p. 16-24
notes.evidence: There are three typical sources of air used to pressurize reciprocating aircraft: supercharger, turbocharger, and enginedriven compressor. Superchargers and turbochargers are installed on reciprocating engines to permit better performance at high altitude by increasing the quantity and pressure of the air in the induction system.

notes.front: Where must a supercharger be located if it is to be used for cabin pressurisation?
notes.back: Upstream of the fuel delivery.
notes.explanation: A radial engine supercharger cannot be used because fuel is added before its impeller compresses the air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Aircraft”, p. 16-24
notes.evidence: Superchargers must be located upstream of the fuel delivery to be used for pressurization. They are found on older reciprocating engine aircraft, including those with radial engines.

notes.front: What is the most common source of pressurisation on modern reciprocating-engine aircraft?
notes.back: The turbocharger (turbosupercharger), driven by engine exhaust gases.
notes.explanation: Using its air for the cabin leaves less for the engine intake, lowering overall engine performance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Aircraft”, p. 16-24
notes.evidence: Turbochargers, sometimes known as turbosuperchargers, are driven by engine exhaust gases. They are the most common source of pressurization on modern reciprocating engine aircraft.

notes.front: What contamination risk do superchargers and turbochargers carry as pressurisation sources?
notes.back: If they malfunction, oil, fuel or exhaust fumes may contaminate the cabin air.
notes.explanation: Both are oil lubricated, and one is part of the intake system while the other is part of the exhaust system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Reciprocating Engine Aircraft”, p. 16-25
notes.evidence: Both superchargers and turbochargers are oil lubricated. The supercharger is part of the fuel intake system and the turbocharger is part of the exhaust system. As such, there is a risk of contamination of cabin air from oil, fuel, or exhaust fumes should a malfunction occur, a shortcoming of these pressurization sources.
