notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Evacuating the System”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: A typical pump used for evacuating an air conditioning system can reduce system pressure to about 29.62 "Hg (gauge pressure). At this pressure, water boils at 45 °F.

notes.front: When must a vapour cycle system be evacuated before recharging?
notes.back: Whenever its charge falls below atmospheric pressure, the refrigerant is lost, or the system is opened.
notes.explanation: Only a few drops of moisture can contaminate the system and freeze in the expansion valve.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Evacuating the System”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: Only a few drops of moisture can contaminate a vapor cycle air conditioning system. If this moisture freezes in the expansion valve, it could completely block the refrigerant flow. Water is removed from the system by evacuation. Anytime the system refrigerant charge falls below atmospheric pressure, the refrigerant is lost, or the system is opened, it must be evacuated before recharging.

notes.front: A vapour cycle system shows bubbles in the sight glass, but its low side still reads well above atmospheric pressure when idle, and it has never been opened. Can refrigerant simply be added?
notes.back: A) Yes; a system that has kept a charge above atmospheric pressure may be topped up without evacuation
notes.choices:
A) Yes; a system that has kept a charge above atmospheric pressure may be topped up without evacuation
B) No; every top-up needs a full evacuation
C) No; the system must first be flushed and the receiver dryer replaced
D) Yes, but only after venting the remaining charge
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: evacuation is required only after the charge falls below atmospheric, is lost, or the system is opened. C is for suspected contamination, such as a failed component. D is illegal and needless venting.
notes.explanation: While system pressure stays above atmospheric, leaks push refrigerant out and keep air and water from getting in.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Evacuating the System”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: As long as a vapor cycle air conditioning system retains a charge higher than atmospheric pressure, any leak forces refrigerant out of the system. The system pressure prevents air (and water vapor) from entering. Therefore, it is permissible to recharge or add refrigerant to a system that has not dropped

notes.front: In vapour cycle servicing, what is the difference between purging the system and evacuating it?
notes.back: Purging empties it of its refrigerant charge into a recovery tank; evacuating (pumping down) draws a vacuum to remove water.
notes.explanation: Purging comes first, before the system is opened; evacuation follows before recharging.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging the System”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: Purging the system means emptying it of its refrigerant charge. Since the refrigerant must be captured, a service cart with this capability should be used. By connecting the hoses to the high side and low side service valves and selecting recover, cart solenoid valves position so that a system purging compressor pumps the refrigerant out of the vapor cycle system and into a recovery tank.

notes.front: When a vapour cycle system is flushed after contamination, what is done with the receiver dryer?
notes.back: It is removed for flushing and a new unit, with fresh filters, is installed.
notes.explanation: Flushing is used when contamination is suspected, such as after a catastrophic component failure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Purging the System”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: When suspicion exists that the system has been contaminated, such as when a component has catastrophically failed, it can be flushed clean. Special fluid flush formulated for vapor cycle air conditioning systems should be used. The receiver dryer is removed from the system for flushing and a new unit is installed, as it contains fresh filters.

notes.front: A good electronic refrigerant leak detector can detect leaks that would lose less than {{c1::1⁄2 ounce}} of refrigerant per year.
notes.explanation: A detector specified for the system’s type of refrigerant should be chosen.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Detectors”, p. 16-54
notes.evidence: A detector specified for the type of refrigerant in the system should be chosen. A good leak detector is sensitive enough to detect leaks that would result in less than 1⁄2 ounce of refrigerant to be lost per year.

notes.front: What should a technician suspect about a vapour cycle system that needs refrigerant added?
notes.back: That it has a leak.
notes.explanation: A system operating normally loses little or no refrigerant.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Detectors”, p. 16-53
notes.evidence: Even the smallest leak in a vapor cycle air conditioning system can cause a loss of refrigerant. When operating normally, little or no refrigerant escapes. A system that requires the addition of refrigerant should be suspected of having a leak.

notes.front: Apart from electronic detectors, what are two other ways of finding refrigerant leaks?
notes.back: A soapy solution that bubbles at a leak, and leak detection dyes, many visible under ultraviolet light.
notes.explanation: Oil forced out of a leak can also leave visible residue, usually under the leaky fitting.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Detectors”, p. 16-54
notes.evidence: Other leak detection methods exist. A soapy solution can also be applied to fittings and inspected for the formation of bubbles indicating a leak. Special leak detection dyes compatible for use with refrigerant can be injected into the vapor cycle system and can be seen when they are forced

notes.front: After all the refrigerant has leaked out, about how much pressure should be put in the system to find the leak?
notes.back: About 50 psi of refrigerant in the high and low sides.
notes.explanation: A partial charge makes the leak detectable without wasting time and refrigerant before the full evacuation that must follow.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Test”, p. 16-55
notes.evidence: To locate the leak point, the system needs to be partially charged with refrigerant so leak detection methods can be employed. About 50 psi of refrigerant in the high and low sides should be sufficient for a leak check.

notes.front: A vapour cycle system has lost its whole charge. The technician finds and repairs the leak using a 50 psi partial charge. What must happen before the full charge?
notes.back: B) Recover the partial charge, then evacuate the system fully
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; add refrigerant until the sight glass clears
B) Recover the partial charge, then evacuate the system fully
C) Run the system for an hour to dry it
D) Add oil only
notes.choicesExplained: A skips the evacuation required after the charge was lost. C cannot remove water the way a vacuum does. D does nothing about air and water that entered.
notes.explanation: When a system loses all its charge, air and water may enter, so full evacuation must follow the repair.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Leak Test”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: When a vapor cycle air conditioning system loses all of its refrigerant charge, air may enter the system. Water may also enter since it is in the air. This means that a full system evacuation must be performed after the leak is found and repaired.

notes.front: In a performance test, with controls at full cold after a few minutes’ running, a thermometer in the evaporator outflow should read {{c1::40–50 °F}}.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer’s instructions say where to place the thermometer and what range is acceptable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Performance Test”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: An ordinary thermometer should read 40–50 °F, with the controls set to full cold after the system has been allowed to operate for a few minutes.

notes.front: What are typical low side and high side pressures in a normally operating vapour cycle system?
notes.back: Low side 10–50 psi; high side 125–250 psi, depending on ambient temperature and design.
notes.explanation: Tests are done at a specified engine rpm with time allowed for the cycle to stabilise.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Performance Test”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: Typically, low side pressure in a vapor cycle system operating normally is 10–50 psi, depending on ambient temperature. High side pressure is between 125 and 250 psi, again, depending on ambient temperature and the design of the system.

notes.front: In a quick feel test of a vapour cycle system, how should the high side, the lines at the receiver dryer and the low side feel?
notes.back: High side warm or hot; both receiver dryer lines the same temperature; low side and evaporator cool.
notes.explanation: Any discrepancy, or visible ice, calls for further investigation.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Feel Test”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: In particular, components and lines in the high side (from the compressor to the expansion valve) should be warm or hot to the touch. The lines on both sides of the receiver dryer should be the same temperature. Low side lines and the evaporator should be cool. Ice should not be visible on the outside of the system.

notes.front: After several minutes at full cold and the specified engine rpm, the air leaving a vapour cycle evaporator measures 64 °F. What does this suggest?
notes.back: B) Performance below the typical range, so the cause should be investigated
notes.choices:
A) Normal performance
B) Performance below the typical range, so the cause should be investigated
C) The system is overcooling
D) The thermometer must be faulty, since 64 °F is normal
notes.choicesExplained: A and D ignore that the typical reading is 40–50 °F. C is the opposite of a reading warmer than the range.
notes.explanation: An ordinary thermometer should read 40–50 °F at the evaporator outflow; warmer air means the system is underperforming.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Performance Test”, p. 16-56
notes.evidence: A key indication of performance is the temperature of the air that is cooled by the evaporator. This can be measured at the air outflow from the evaporator or at a nearby delivery duct outlet. An ordinary thermometer should read 40–50 °F,

notes.front: A standard amount of oil to add to a vapour cycle system is approximately {{c1::1⁄4 ounce}} for each pound of refrigerant.
notes.explanation: Extra oil may be needed when a component is changed, to replace what is trapped in the old unit; the specified oil is always used.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Visual Inspection”, p. 16-55
notes.evidence: Typically, 1⁄4 ounce of oil is added for each pound of refrigerant added to the system. When changing a component, additional oil may need to be added to replace that which is trapped in the replaced unit. Always use the oil specified in the manufacturer’s maintenance manual.

notes.front: When should a vapour cycle system be charged, and how is the right amount ensured?
notes.back: Immediately after evacuation is complete, pre-weighing the refrigerant or setting its weight on the servicing cart.
notes.explanation: The maintenance manual gives the charge weight and the type and amount of oil.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Charging the System”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: Pre-weighing the refrigerant or setting the refrigerant weight into the servicing cart input ensures the system is filled to capacity. Charging a vapor cycle air conditioning system should be undertaken immediately after evacuation of the system is completed.

notes.front: When charging, refrigerant is first released into the high side. What shows it is passing through the expansion valve?
notes.back: The low side gauge begins to indicate pressure.
notes.explanation: The only path from high to low side runs through the valve’s tiny orifice.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Charging the System”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: First, refrigerant is released into the high side of the system. Observe the low side gauge. When the low side gauge begins to indicate pressure, it is known that refrigerant is passing through the tiny orifice in the expansion valve.

notes.front: Partway through charging, flow into the high side has stopped. The engine is at high idle with full cool selected. How should the rest of the charge be put in?
notes.back: B) Close the high side valve and let the compressor draw the rest in through the low side
notes.choices:
A) Keep forcing liquid into the high side
B) Close the high side valve and let the compressor draw the rest in through the low side
C) Open both service valves fully and invert the container on the low side
D) Stop; the system is already fully charged
notes.choicesExplained: A cannot work once pressure has built in the high side. C risks sending liquid into the compressor inlet. D assumes a full charge when the weighed amount has not yet gone in.
notes.explanation: The compressor must draw in the remainder, and a major concern is to keep liquid refrigerant out of its inlet.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Charging the System”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: To complete the charge of the system, refrigerant needs to be drawn in by the compressor. A major concern is to avoid damage to the compressor by having liquid refrigerant enter the compressor inlet. After the initial release of refrigerant into the high side, the high side service valve is closed, and the remaining charge is made through the low side service

notes.front: When charging with a manifold set, what is done after opening the refrigerant container and before refrigerant enters the system?
notes.back: Loosen the centre hose connection at the manifold to let the air in the hose escape.
notes.explanation: Bleeding the hose keeps air, which carries water, out of the system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Charging the System”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: After opening the valve on the container (or puncturing the seal on a small can), the center hose connection on the manifold set should be loosened to allow air in the hose to escape. Once the air is bled out of the hose, the refrigerant can enter the system through whichever service valve is opened.

notes.front: Which agency requires certification of technicians who work with vapour cycle refrigerant and equipment?
notes.back: The Environmental Protection Agency.
notes.explanation: The certification ensures safe compliance with current regulations.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Technician Certification”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: The EPA requires certification of technicians that work with vapor cycle air conditioning refrigerant and equipment to ensure safe compliance with current regulations.

notes.front: A certificated airframe mechanic with no refrigerant certification is asked to recover and recharge a vapour cycle system. What are the options?
notes.back: C) Obtain the required certification, or refer the work to a specialist shop
notes.choices:
A) Do it, since the mechanic certificate covers all aircraft systems
B) Do it, provided the refrigerant is vented outdoors
C) Obtain the required certification, or refer the work to a specialist shop
D) Do it under another mechanic’s supervision
notes.choicesExplained: A overlooks the separate certification the Environmental Protection Agency requires. B adds illegal venting of R-12, and poor practice for any refrigerant. D is not an option the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: The handbook says technicians can obtain certification or refer vapour cycle work to shops that specialise in it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Technician Certification”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: The EPA requires certification of technicians that work with vapor cycle air conditioning refrigerant and equipment to ensure safe compliance with current regulations. Aircraft technicians can obtain certification or can refer vapor cycle air conditioning work to shops that specialize in this work.

notes.front: Which refrigerant-related risk do the Airman Certification Standards expect an airframe applicant to identify and mitigate?
notes.back: Recovery of vapour-cycle refrigerant.
notes.explanation: The standards also list following the manufacturer’s recommended servicing procedures, including refrigerant types.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (2021), Section II, Subject G, Environmental Systems, Risk Management elements R2 and R5, p. 28
notes.evidence: AM.II.G.R2 Recovery of vapor-cycle refrigerant. AM.II.G.R3 Handling or performing maintenance on, chemical oxygen generating systems. AM.II.G.R4 Storage, handling, and use of compressed gas cylinder and high pressure systems. AM.II.G.R5 Manufacturer's recommended servicing procedures, including refrigerant types.

notes.front: How do pressurised aircraft with air cycle systems get warm air for the cabin?
notes.back: They mix bleed air with the cold air from the ACM expansion turbine.
notes.explanation: At high altitude the outside air can be well below 0 °F, so cabin heat is more than a luxury.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Bleed Air Systems”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: Temperatures at high altitudes in which aircraft operate can be well below 0 °F. Combined with seasonally cold temperatures, this makes heating the cabin more than just a luxury. Pressurized aircraft that use air cycle air conditioning systems mix bleed air with cold air produced by the air cycle machine expansion turbine to obtain warm air for the cabin.

notes.front: How do some turbine aircraft without air cycle systems heat the cabin with bleed air?
notes.back: Bleed air is mixed with ambient air or cabin return air and ducted through the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Mixing, flow control and shutoff valves worked from the flight deck manage the mix.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Bleed Air Systems”, p. 16-57
notes.evidence: Some turbine-powered aircraft not equipped with air cycle systems still make use of engine compressor bleed air to heat the cabin. Various arrangements exist. The bleed air is mixed with ambient air, or cabin return air, and distributed throughout the aircraft via ducting.

notes.front: A turboprop without air cycle air conditioning heats its cabin by mixing bleed air with cabin return air. The cabin stays cold with heat selected. Where should the mechanic look?
notes.back: A) The valves, ducting and flight deck controls of the bleed air heat system
notes.choices:
A) The valves, ducting and flight deck controls of the bleed air heat system
B) The combustion heater’s spark plug
C) The exhaust shroud for cracks
D) The vapour cycle compressor clutch
notes.choicesExplained: B belongs to a combustion heater this aircraft does not have. C is the heat source on piston aircraft with shroud heaters. D is part of a cooling system.
notes.explanation: The handbook says bleed air heating systems are simple and work well as long as the valves, ducting and controls work.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Bleed Air Systems”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: All of these bleed air heating systems are simple and function well, as long as the valves, ducting, and controls are in operational condition.

notes.front: Why are electric cabin heaters not very common, and when are they useful?
notes.back: They take a large share of generator output; they are useful on the ground, on ground power, to preheat the cabin.
notes.explanation: On ground power they warm the cabin before boarding without taxing the aircraft’s electrical system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Electric Heating Systems”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: of the aircraft’s generator output, which is better dedicated to the operation of other electrical devices. For this reason, they are not very common. However, their use on the ground when powered by a ground electrical power source preheats the cabin before passengers board and does not tax the electrical system.

notes.front: Which aircraft mostly use exhaust shroud heaters?
notes.back: Most single-engine light aircraft.
notes.explanation: The system is simple and uses exhaust heat that would otherwise be wasted.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: Most single-engine light aircraft use exhaust shroud heating systems to heat the cabin.

notes.front: What is the major concern with exhaust shroud heaters?
notes.back: Exhaust gases contaminating cabin air: even the slightest manifold crack could send in enough carbon monoxide to be fatal.
notes.explanation: Strict inspection procedures exist to minimise this threat.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: A major concern of exhaust shroud heat systems is the possibility that exhaust gases could contaminate the cabin air. Even the slightest crack in an exhaust manifold could send enough carbon monoxide into the cabin to be fatal. Strict inspection procedures are in place to minimize this threat.

notes.front: How are exhaust systems under heater shrouds usually checked for leaks, and how often can this be required?
notes.back: Pressurise the exhaust with air and check with soapy solution, or pressurise it submerged in water; as often as every 100 hours.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the frequency of exhaust heat leak detection can be every 100 hours.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: Most involve pressurizing the exhaust system with air, while inspecting for leaks with a soapy solution. Some require the exhaust to be removed and pressurized while submerged under water to detect any leaks. Frequency of exhaust heat leak detection can be every 100 hours.

notes.front: Why do welded studs on an exhaust muffler deserve attention at inspection?
notes.back: Each weld point is a potential leak location.
notes.explanation: The studs are added to increase heat transfer to the cabin air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-59
notes.evidence: For example, an exhaust muffler may have numerous welded studs attached, which increase heat transfer to the cabin air. Each weld point is a location for a potential leak.

notes.front: What should every aircraft with an exhaust shroud heating system carry in the flight deck, regardless of age or condition?
notes.back: A carbon monoxide detection device.
notes.explanation: The onset of carbon monoxide poisoning can be very subtle, so the crew needs a warning.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-59
notes.evidence: Regardless of age or condition, aircraft with exhaust shroud heating systems should contain a carbon monoxide detection device in the flight deck.

notes.front: A pilot of a single-engine piston aircraft reports that the flight deck carbon monoxide tab darkened whenever cabin heat was on. What should the mechanic suspect and do?
notes.back: B) A cracked exhaust manifold inside the heater shroud; leak check the exhaust before further use of cabin heat
notes.choices:
A) A faulty tab; replace it and return the aircraft to service
B) A cracked exhaust manifold inside the heater shroud; leak check the exhaust before further use of cabin heat
C) Low oxygen pressure; service the oxygen system
D) An overcharged vapour cycle system
notes.choicesExplained: A assumes the detector is wrong without finding the source. C has no link to carbon monoxide. D is a cooling system and not a combustion source.
notes.explanation: The handbook stresses finding the source of any carbon monoxide detected; with a shroud heater, a manifold crack is the known path into the cabin.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Exhaust Shroud Heaters”, p. 16-58
notes.evidence: Even the slightest crack in an exhaust manifold could send enough carbon monoxide into the cabin to be fatal.

notes.front: In a combustion heater, how is combustion air kept apart from the air sent to the cabin?
notes.back: Combustion air burns in the airtight inner chamber and exhausts overboard; cabin air passes between chamber and outer shroud.
notes.explanation: The ventilating air picks up heat by convection from the outside of the chamber.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Combustion Heaters”, p. 16-59
notes.evidence: The correct amount of fuel and air are ignited in the air-tight inner chamber. The exhaust from combustion is funneled overboard. Ambient air is directed between the combustion chamber and the outer shroud. It absorbs the combustion heat by convection and is channeled into the cabin.

notes.front: In a combustion heater, what ensures the right quantity and pressure of combustion air?
notes.back: A blower, sometimes with regulators or a relief valve.
notes.explanation: The combustion air is scooped from outside or from the heater’s compartment and kept completely separate from the ventilating air.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Combustion Air System”, p. 16-59
notes.evidence: A blower ensures that the correct quantity and pressure of air are sent into the chamber. Some units have regulators or a relief valve to ensure these parameters. The combustion air is completely separate from the air that is warmed and sent into the cabin.

notes.front: What is ventilating air in a combustion heater, and how does it flow on the ground and in flight?
notes.back: The air warmed and sent to the cabin; a squat-switch-controlled fan draws it in on the ground, ram air in flight.
notes.explanation: Once airborne, ram air flow is enough, so the fan stops.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Ventilating Air System”, p. 16-59
notes.evidence: Ventilating air is the name of the air that is warmed and sent into the cabin. Typically, it comes into the combustion heater through a ram air intake. When the aircraft is on the ground, a ventilating air fan controlled by a landing gear squat switch operates to draw in the air. Once airborne, the fan ceases to operate as the ram air flow is sufficient.

notes.front: How does fuel reach a combustion heater?
notes.back: A constant pressure pump with relief valve draws it from an aircraft tank through a filter to a main solenoid valve.
notes.explanation: The cabin heater switch and three safety switches control that solenoid.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Fuel System”, p. 16-60
notes.evidence: As mentioned, fuel for the combustion heater is drawn from an aircraft fuel tank. A constant pressure fuel pump with relief valve pulls the fuel through a filter. A main solenoid valve downstream delivers the fuel to the unit.

notes.front: Which combustion heater safety switch keeps the fuel solenoid closed when there is not enough ventilating airflow?
notes.back: The duct limit switch.
notes.explanation: Without enough ventilating air the unit cannot stay within its correct operating temperature.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Fuel System”, p. 16-60
notes.evidence: The first safety switch is a duct limit switch that keeps the valve closed should the unit not have enough ventilating airflow to keep it within the correct operating temperature range.

notes.front: Which combustion heater safety switch must sense pressure from the combustion air fan before fuel can flow?
notes.back: The pressure switch.
notes.explanation: Fuel goes to the chamber only if there is air there to mix with it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Fuel System”, p. 16-60
notes.evidence: The second is a pressure switch that must sense pressure from the combustion air fan to allow the solenoid to open. Fuel is delivered to the combustion chamber only if there is air there with which it can be mixed.

notes.front: In a combustion heater, what does the overheat switch do, and what follows when it trips?
notes.back: Set hotter than the duct limit switch, it cuts fuel before an unwanted fire; a flight deck light comes on and the heater cannot be restarted.
notes.explanation: The heater stays off until maintenance determines the cause.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Safety Features”, p. 16-61
notes.evidence: unwanted fire occurs. When this switch activates, a light is illuminated in the flight deck and the heater cannot be restarted until maintenance determines the cause.

notes.front: How does a combustion heater cycle on and off in normal operation?
notes.back: The thermostat opens and closes a secondary fuel control solenoid at the combustion chamber entrance.
notes.explanation: Ventilating air keeps circulating between cycles and carries heat away.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Fuel System”, p. 16-60
notes.evidence: The valve opens and closes on command from the combustion heater thermostat. During normal operation, the heater cycles on and off by opening and closing this solenoid at the entrance to the combustion chamber.

notes.front: How is the fuel in a combustion heater ignited?
notes.back: An ignition unit steps up aircraft voltage to fire a spark plug in the chamber, continuously while activated.
notes.explanation: Older heaters use vibrator-type units and modern ones electronic ignition; the proper spark plug is essential.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Ignition System”, p. 16-60
notes.evidence: Most combustion heaters have an ignition unit designed to receive aircraft voltage and step it up to fire a spark plug located in the combustion chamber. Older combustion heaters use vibrator-type ignition units. Modern units have electronic ignition.

notes.front: What does routine combustion heater maintenance consist of?
notes.back: Cleaning filters, checking spark plug wear and making sure inlets are not plugged.
notes.explanation: All of it follows the aircraft manufacturer’s instructions and the heater maker’s guidelines, including overhaul times.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 16-61
notes.evidence: Maintenance of combustion heaters consists of routine items, such as cleaning filters, checking spark plug wear, and ensuring inlets are not plugged. All maintenance and inspection of combustion heaters should be accomplished in accordance with the aircraft manufacturer’s instructions.

notes.front: When should a combustion heater be inspected, and what should be looked for closely?
notes.back: On the manufacturer’s schedule or when a malfunction is suspected; any fuel leaks or cracks in the chamber or shroud.
notes.explanation: Inlets and outlets should be clear, controls free, and all components secure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 16-61
notes.evidence: Inspection of the combustion heater should be performed on schedule as provided by the manufacturer or whenever a malfunction is suspected. Inlets and outlets should be clear. All controls should be checked for freedom of operation and function. Close observation for any sign of fuel leaks or cracks in the combustion chamber and/or shroud should be made.

notes.front: A combustion heater shut down in flight, a flight deck light came on, and it will not restart. The pilot asks for it to be reset so he can leave. What is right?
notes.back: D) The overheat switch tripped; find the cause before the heater is used again
notes.choices:
A) Reset it and release the aircraft
B) The duct limit switch tripped, so it resets itself when cool
C) Replace the thermostat, which caused the shutdown
D) The overheat switch tripped; find the cause before the heater is used again
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the lockout, which stays until maintenance finds the cause. B misreads it: the latched light and lockout come from the overheat switch. C guesses a part without investigating.
notes.explanation: When the overheat switch activates, a light comes on and the heater cannot restart until maintenance determines the cause.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Safety Features”, p. 16-61
notes.evidence: When this switch activates, a light is illuminated in the flight deck and the heater cannot be restarted until maintenance determines the cause.

notes.front: On the ground, a combustion heater keeps cutting off shortly after lighting, but works normally in flight. Which fault best explains this?
notes.back: A) A failed ventilating air fan, so the duct limit switch cuts fuel
notes.choices:
A) A failed ventilating air fan, so the duct limit switch cuts fuel
B) A failed combustion air blower
C) A cracked exhaust manifold
D) A fuel solenoid stuck open
notes.choicesExplained: B would stop it lighting at all, as the pressure switch needs blower pressure. C is an exhaust shroud heater problem. D would keep fuel flowing, not cut it off.
notes.explanation: On the ground only the fan moves ventilating air; ram air takes over in flight, and too little ventilating air trips the duct limit switch.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 16, Cabin Environmental Control Systems, “Safety Features”, p. 16-61
notes.evidence: As stated, a duct limit switch cuts off fuel to the heater when there is not enough airflow to keep the heater duct below a preset temperature. This is usually caused by a lack of ventilating air flow.
